title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
For a Claude session asked to add a style (“add a samba”, “a second-line groove”, “a gospel 6/8”). Read this first, then the header comments of the files it names. NOTES.org beside this file is the history of the band and its open questions.


A style is a row in styles in catalog.js: a name, a group (the genre heading in the Style menu), and defaults that belong together.
{ id:"bossa", label:"Bossa nova", group:"Latin", genres:"Bossa nova, slow samba",
  feel:"straight", bass:"bossa", rhythm:"bossa", drums:"bossa", voicing:JAZZV,
  desc:"Root-and-fifth bass with pickups, a two-bar comping pattern and the bossa clave." }

bass, rhythm, drums are ids of entries in the bass, comp and drums lists of the same file. rhythm may be several joined by + (a blend).
voicing is { piano, guitar }: a voicing style id for each (PLAINV, STRUMV, JAZZV are ready-made).
Optional: sound ({ bass:"upright"|"electric", cymbal:"ride"|"hat"|"bell", piano, guitar, lead, kit }), where piano and guitar are sound ids from sounds.js (BandSounds.sounds("guitar") lists them: jazz, steel, nylon, clean and distorted electric), push (chords anticipate), time ({ feel:"half", parts }), ext:true (unmarked extensions on offer). A style with no sound gets upright bass, ride, piano, jazz guitar.

A style made only of parts that already exist is one line in styles plus the fit lists (step 3). Most requests need at least one new part. Decide that first: listen in your head to what the bass, the chord instrument and the drums each play in that music, and check each against the existing entries before writing a new one.




Write the new parts, each in its own engine file. Copy the nearest existing pattern and read the comment block above the table you are adding to.

Bass line: LINES in bass.js (a fixed figure over the chord’s root, fifth, octave).
Comping rhythm: GRID in comp.js for a set pattern, FIG for a one-bar swing figure.
Drum groove: GROOVES in drums.js (bars for 4/4, threeBars for 3/4, triplet for 12/8 feels).
Positions are beats from 0; x.5 is the off-beat eighth (swung by the player unless the event says straight:true). Velocities are 0..1 and the player scales them by the band’s intensity.
Use ctx.phrase.bar (0..3) to shape four-bar phrases and ctx.intensity for how hard the band is playing. phraseDyn, leanDyn and spread in comp.js are the shared dynamic shaping: use them rather than fixed velocities.
Every pattern must cope with 3/4 and with a bar holding two chords. The tests check both.

Describe each new part in catalog.js: an entry in bass, comp or drums with id, label, feel (swing, straight or any), group, tags and a desc that says what is played on which beats, in a musician’s words. The desc is shown on the page and on the Accompaniment Styles page.
Say where each part fits: add its id to FITS.bass, FITS.comp or FITS.drums with the style ids it belongs in (your new one, and any existing style it also suits). Locked, a menu lists only what fits the chosen style, so a part missing from FITS cannot be chosen. Add the new style id to the voicing lists it should offer (JAZZ, POP, PLAIN, or a VOICE row).
Add the style row to styles, in its group. The id is permanent: saved setups, links and song files name it. Never rename one.
Tests (plain node, run from the test’s own directory):

tests/band/pat/t_patterns.js runs every style and option against every meter. It has a want table of where chords must land for set patterns; add your rhythm there.
tests/band/pat/t_pop.js lists the style ids of some groups in order; update the list if you added to one.
tests/band/styles/t_sections.js, tests/band/fills/t_fills.js, tests/band/meter/t_change.js must still pass.

Publish it to the pages. In tools/_backing-track.qmd and tools/_accomp-styles.qmd, raise the ?v= number on every script you changed (browsers cache them). Then quarto render tools/backing-track.qmd and check that .gitignore did not change (Quarto appends to it). The lyrics site copies the engine: bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh.
Say what was not verified. Nothing here can be listened to from a terminal. Report the pattern in beats, what the tests cover, and that it needs ears. Do not commit unless asked.





The Style menu of the Backing Track page; ?style=id in its address.
A tune’s ABC: %%style bossa nova above the first P: line (the whole tune).
One section: %%style bossa nova on the line under its P: line, or "^style bossa nova" in a bar (from that bar to the next section; "^style none" ends it early). The form bar carries style, and BandCatalog.sectionOpts turns it into the options for those bars. Single parts can follow the name: %%style Swing; voicing drop2; rhythm charleston; bass two; drums funk; feel straight. The comping moves to the instrument the style is built around (sound.lead), if it has one. The page’s blend sliders and walk amount do not apply inside such a section. On the Backing Track page the Band menus change to a section’s settings as it starts, and a change made there stays with that section (opts.sectionOverrides, which the player puts before the section’s style).
Two built-in setups in presets.js (“Style demo: …”) tour the jazz and the pop, rock and country styles a section at a time. Add a new style to the one it belongs in.
A lyrics-site song file (~/Projects/carols/site/extra/*.cho): {style: carol} above the first heading for the song, or under a heading for that section. See the top of tools/chordpro.py there.
A name matches an id, a menu label, or part of a label, ignoring case.





Plain JS globals, no build step, no dependencies. Match the comment density and voice of the file.
A new option is opt-in: an existing style must sound exactly as it did, and an option left unset must not draw from the random number generator (the tests compare runs).
Sample sets are named only in sounds.js. A new sound is one entry there (family, label, zones, and an optional amp chain); the Comping menu, the player and styleOpts pick it up from that entry. Add its General MIDI program to PROGRAM in midi.js, and its samples to tests/band/meter/fetch-samples.js.
Write descriptions for a music teacher: beats and instruments, no code words.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text: The quarter note gets one beat in common time. In a 4/4 measure you can fit four of them — one per beat. We count them simply: 1 – 2 – 3 – 4.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text:
Hear it, then say it
Before reading a single quarter note, you should be able to audiate a steady beat — feel it internally — and chant a neutral syllable on each beat. Only after the sound is secure do we attach the symbol.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text:
Practice steps

Tap a steady beat with your foot.
Chant “bah” on each tap for four beats.
Now look at four quarter notes and chant them while tapping.

When you’re ready, head to Practice → Rhythm Patterns and play a few quarter-note patterns. Your time on this page and your plays over there are both recorded automatically.






Tip



This page is being timed. Stay as long as you need; switch tabs and the timer pauses. Come back and it resumes.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text: Tonal patterns are short groups of pitches we learn by ear first, with solfège, before we ever name a key signature. The foundation is the major tonic and dominant.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Stepwise motion
The most basic tonal pattern is stepwise: Do – Re – Mi – Fa – Sol and back down. Sing it on a neutral syllable first, then with solfège, then connect it to what you see on the staff.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Tonic and dominant

Tonic (Do – Mi – Sol): the “home” chord, restful.
Dominant (Sol – Ti – Re): the “tension” chord that wants to resolve home.

Hearing the difference between these two is the single most important tonal skill in beginning band.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Practice steps

Sing Do, then find Sol.
Sing the tonic arpeggio, then the dominant.
Go to Practice → Tonal Patterns and play major stepwise patterns, singing along with solfège.

            calypso
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beats 1 and 3, light chords on every upbeat — the Trinidadian and Jamaican "afterbeat." Mento is the Jamaican root form; calypso developed in Trinidad. Both patterns flowed into ska and reggae.

            Caribbean
            Roots
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Samba
            samba
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Surdo-style kick on beats 2 and 4 (absent on beat 1), snare on beat 3, hi-hat fills every eighth. The rhythmic foundation of Brazilian carnival parade music; transferred to the drum kit from the samba bateria.

            Brazilian
            Drum set
            Bateria
          
        

        
          
            Mambo
            mambo
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on beat 1 and the "and-of-3" (a clave-derived anticipation), snare on beat 3, hi-hats throughout. Developed in 1940s Havana by Dámaso Pérez Prado; bridged Cuban son and American big-band.

            Cuban
            Drum set
            Full band
          
        

      
    

    
      Funk & R&B
      

        
          
            Funk
            funk
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on beats 1 and 3; syncopated snare on the "and-of-2" and "and-of-4"; hi-hat anchors the eighth-note pulse. James Brown's drummers — Clyde Stubblefield and John "Jabo" Starks — defined this feel.
          
            Funk
            R&B
            Drum set
          
        

        
          
            Half-time feel
            halftime
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Snare moves to beat 3 (rather than 2 and 4), making 2 bars feel like 1. Common in hip-hop, stadium rock, and ballad bridges where the tempo needs to feel broader without actually slowing down.
          
            Pop
            Hip-hop
            Rock
            Drum set
          
        

        
          
            New Orleans second line
            secondline
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on every beat; snare on the "and-of-1" and "and-of-3." The marching parade groove of New Orleans brass bands; adopted by jazz funk, R&B, and rock drummers (the Meters, Allen Toussaint, Dr. John).
          
            Funk
            New Orleans
            Jazz
            Drum set
            Marching
          
        

      
    

    
      Waltz & Dance
      

        
          
            Waltz
            waltz
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beat 1, chord on beats 2 and 3. The universal dance-band formula for 3/4 time. The slight delay before the chord creates the characteristic lilt that distinguishes waltz from a march.
          
            Dance
            Classical
            Piano
            Orchestra
          
        

        
          
            Viennese waltz
            viennese
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          A short downbeat chord followed by slightly-early beats 2 and 3 (the "anticipated" Viennese lilt). The elastic timing distinguishes the Strauss concert hall waltz from the plainer ballroom waltz.
          
            Dance
            Classical
            Romantic
            Orchestra
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Boom-chick
            oompah
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root on the downbeat, chord on every other beat. The engine of polka, march, and German dance-band styles; derived from tuba–horn interplay in brass ensembles.
          
            Folk
            Polka
            March
            Brass
            Accordion
          
        

      
    

    
      Folk & Country
      

        
          
            Folk — alternating bass
            folk
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Alternating root–fifth bass note with a chord on the off-beat. The defining guitar and banjo accompaniment pattern in American folk, bluegrass, and country; also called the "Carter scratch."
          
            Folk
            Country
            Bluegrass
            Guitar
            Banjo
          
        

      
    

    
      Pop & Rock
      

        
          
            Pop / ballad
            pop
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beats 1 and 3, steady quarter-note chords on all beats. The most common piano and keyboard pattern in popular music since the 1950s.
          
            Pop
            Rock
            Piano
            Keyboard
          
        

        
          
            Driving 8ths
            driving8
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Steady eighth-note chords with no gaps. Propulsive and energetic; fills every subdivision. Found across rock, country, and pop guitar — sometimes called a "strum pattern."
          
            Rock
            Country
            Pop
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Offbeat chords
            offbeat
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Chord only on the off-beats, silence on the downbeats. The defining rhythmic gesture of ska and reggae; known as the "skank" or "chop." In reggae, the kick lands on beat 3 (the "one-drop").
          
            Ska
            Reggae
            Guitar
            Keyboard
          
        

      
    

    
      Classical & Piano
      

        
          
            Block chords
            block
            any
            ▶
          
          
          All voices together on every beat, sustained until the next chord. The simplest possible accompaniment; used for chorale writing, teaching chord shapes, and very slow tempos.
          
            Classical
            Chorale
            Piano
            Keyboard
          
        

        
          
            Piano arpeggio ↑
            arpflow
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Rising arpeggios through the full bar (root–third–fifth–octave). Characteristic of Romantic-era piano writing and nocturne accompaniment; adds forward motion when chord changes are sparse.
          
            Classical
            Romantic
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Arpeggio (root–5th)
            arpcell
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root and fifth as individual tones in a repeating per-beat cell. Creates a light, open texture that suggests harmonic motion without dense block chords; useful for harp or guitar figuration.

            Pop
            Harp
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Bass line (roots)
            bassroot
            any

      Piano & Keyboard
      
        
          Block chordsblockany
          Sustained block voicing on every beat. The starting point for learning chord shapes and for chorale-style writing.
          ClassicalChorale
        
        
          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Left-hand bass on 1, right-hand chord on 2–3. The standard piano waltz texture from Chopin through the ballroom repertoire.
          DanceClassical
        
        
          Pop / balladpopany
          Bass on 1 and 3, chords on every beat. Ubiquitous in pop piano; easy to adapt to either hands-together or stride-style playing.
          PopRock
        
        
          Piano arpeggio ↑arpflow4/4
          Rising broken chord through the full bar. Nocturne and ballad texture; standard left-hand figure in Romantic piano writing.
          ClassicalRomantic
        
        
          Viennese waltzviennese3/4
          Elastic 3/4 with the characteristic early-beat anticipation. Strauss orchestra and salon piano repertoire.
          DanceClassical
        
        
          Jazz Charlestoncharleston4/4
          Syncopated 4/4 comping with a chord on beat 1 and the and-of-2. Common in Stride, Swing, and mainstream jazz piano.
          JazzSwing
        
        
          Jazz waltzjazzwaltz3/4
          Swung bass on 1, light chord on 3. The texture of jazz piano trios playing in 3 — Evans, Peterson, Monk.
          JazzBebop
        
      
    

    
      Guitar & Plucked Strings
      
        
          Folk — alternating bassfolkany
          Thumb alternates root–fifth in the bass; fingers strum the chord on the off-beat. The foundational fingerpicking and flatpicking pattern in folk, bluegrass, and country guitar.
          FolkCountryBluegrass
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving8any
          Steady downstroke eighth notes, no rests. The strum pattern behind countless rock, country, and pop songs.
          RockCountryPop
        
        
          Offbeat chordsoffbeatany
          The ska/reggae "skank": chord only between the beats. In reggae the downstroke is muted, leaving only the upstroke chop.
          SkaReggae
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Tresillo bass with off-beat chords. João Gilberto's original bossa guitar part is the blueprint; the pattern is also widely adapted to keyboard.
          LatinBrazilianJazz
        
        
          Arpeggio (root–5th)arpcellany
          Open-voiced ascending tones per beat. Evokes harp, classical guitar, and lute figuration; widely used in Renaissance and Baroque lute tablature.
          ClassicalPop
        
      
    

    
      Brass & Ensemble
      
        
          Boom-chickoompahany
          Tuba carries the root on 1; horns answer with the chord on 2 (and 4). The pattern maps directly to the brass section interplay in polka bands, march bands, and German Blasmusik.
          PolkaMarchFolk
        
        
          Tangotango4/4
          Habanera cell in the bass with syncopated upper chords. In Argentine tango this interplay moves between bandoneón and piano; in orchestral tango (Piazzolla) it drives the entire ensemble.
          LatinArgentine
        
      
    

    
      Bass & Foundation
      
        
          Bass line (roots)bassrootany
          Root note only, no chords. Use this when practicing bass lines in isolation, or when the melody is dense enough to imply the harmony on its own.
          TeachingMinimal
        
      
    

    
      Drum Set
      
        
          Backbeatbackbeat4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The universal pop and rock groove; the first drum pattern most students encounter.
          PopRock
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving84/4
          Continuous eighth notes on the hi-hat with backbeat snare. Energetic pop and rock feel; common in anthemic and uptempo styles.
          PopRock
        
        
          Ska / reggae (one-drop)ska4/4
          Kick displaced to beat 3; snare and hi-hat emphasise the off-beats. The rhythmic foundation of ska, rocksteady, and roots reggae.
          ReggaeSka
        
        
          Swing — ride cymbalswing_ride4/4
          Swung ride pattern with kick and snare on beats 2 and 4. The standard jazz ride pattern from Swing through bebop.
          JazzSwing
        
        
          Swing — hi-hatswing_hats4/4
          Swung quarter-note hi-hat pulse; lighter texture than ride-cymbal swing. Used in small-group jazz and ballad settings.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Swing — open hi-hatswing_hats_open4/4
          Swung hi-hat opening on beats 2 and 4; airy, washy texture. Common in contemporary jazz and fusion where the drummer wants more cymbal wash than the closed-hat version.
          JazzFusion
        
        
          Swing — brushesswing_brushes4/4
          Wire-brush swirl with soft backbeat. Quiet jazz trio and intimate club setting; the standard brush technique for standards and ballads.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Jazz waltz — ridejazzwaltz_ride3/4
          Swung ride in 3; kick on beat 1, light snare elsewhere. The jazz-waltz drum feel behind Bill Evans, Miles Davis, and the post-bop trio repertoire.
          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Jazz waltz — hi-hatjazzwaltz_hats3/4
          Closed hi-hat pulse in 3 with a light swing feel; more understated than the ride-cymbal version. Used in intimate trio settings where the drummer wants less projection.
          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Ride cymbal tresillo with side-stick; the drum kit adaptation of Brazilian percussion. Foundational in bossa nova and samba-jazz.
          LatinBossa
        
        
          Tango (habanera)tango4/4
          Habanera kick cell with closed hi-hat. The rhythmic engine of Argentine tango and early-20th-century Latin dance music.
          LatinTango
        
        
          Son montuno (clave)montuno4/4
          Cuban clave rhythm on the kick; snare and hi-hat fill the groove. The drum kit version of the son montuno pattern.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Kick on beat 1, hi-hat on 2 and 3. Straightforward triple-meter groove for waltzes, country, and folksong accompaniment.
          DanceFolk
        
        
          Compound (6/8)compound66/8
          Kick on the two main beats, hi-hat subdivisions filling the compound pulse. Used in jigs, compound-feel pop, and gospel 6/8.
          FolkGospel
        
        
          Half-time feelhalftime4/4
          Snare on beat 3 only; kick and hi-hat fill the rest. Makes the bar feel twice as wide without changing tempo. Widely used in hip-hop, stadium rock, and ballad bridges.
          PopHip-hopRock
        
        
          Funkfunk4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3; syncopated snare on the "and-of-2" and "and-of-4"; hi-hat on all eighths. The foundational James Brown / Clyde Stubblefield groove.
          FunkR&B
        
        
          New Orleans second linesecondline4/4
          Kick on every beat, snare on the upbeats of 1 and 3. The marching street-parade groove; adopted by the Meters, Dr. John, and rock drummers worldwide.
          FunkNew Orleans
        
        
          Sambasamba4/4
          Surdo kick on beats 2 and 4; snare on beat 3; hi-hat throughout. The drum kit adaptation of the samba bateria; common in Brazilian jazz and fusion.
          LatinBrazilian
        
        
          Mambomambo4/4
          Kick on beat 1 and the "and-of-3" (a clave-derived anticipation); snare on beat 3. The driving groove of 1940s Havana; ancestor of modern salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Calypso / mentocalypso4/4
          Floating kick (no downbeat on 1); side-stick on beat 3; hi-hat emphasises the upbeats. The Trinidadian and Jamaican afterbeat; ancestral to ska and reggae.
          CaribbeanReggae
        
      
    

    
      Hand Percussion
      
        
          Bongo — martillobongo_martillo4/4
          Steady eighth-note alternation between hi and lo bongo; the "hammer" pattern. The default timekeeping groove in Cuban son and salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Bongo — quarterbongo_slow4/4
          Quarter-note hi/lo alternation; a relaxed, open texture. Works well as a simplified bongo part for classroom or beginner settings.
          LatinTeaching
        
        
          Conga — tumbaoconga_tumbao4/4
          Open tone on the and-of-4, muted tones elsewhere. The foundational Cuban conga pattern; ubiquitous in salsa and son.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — tumbao (dense)conga_tumbao_dense4/4
          Eight-note tumbao with slap and open tone variations; a fuller, more active feel than the standard four-note version.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — sonconga_son4/4
          Alternating lo-conga open tones across the bar; simpler and more open than the tumbao. Common in son cubano and early salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — waltzconga_waltz3/4
          Conga tones on the three main beats in 3/4; pairs with Latin waltz and compound-feel songs.
          LatinWaltz
        
        
          Conga — 6/8conga_6_86/8
          Open and muted conga tones across the compound-triple pulse. Works with 6/8 Afro-Cuban styles and compound jigs.
          LatinAfro-Cuban

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text: A dot adds half the value of the note again. A dotted half note (normally two beats) becomes three beats. A dotted quarter becomes one-and-a-half.

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text:
The dotted-quarter-plus-eighth figure
The classic figure is a dotted quarter followed by an eighth — the “long- short” pattern you hear at the start of countless tunes. It’s tricky because the eighth note lands on the and of beat two, not on a beat.

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text:
Practice steps

Chant a steady “1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &”.
Hold the dotted quarter across “1 & 2”, then say the eighth on “&”.
Try it slowly, then bring it up to tempo.

Then go to Practice → Tunes and find a tune that uses this figure. Play it a few times and listen for the long-short.






Tip



Notice this lesson tracks separately from the quarter-note lesson — the report will show your time on each page, not just “lessons” as a lump.

title: The tonewheel organ
text:
The band’s hammond sound (sounds.js), the organist’s pedal and switch (organist in comp.js), and the panel on the Backing Track page. Written 2026-10-10. Nobody has listened to it. Every level and rule below is either taken from a source (linked) or is a first guess, and the two are kept apart so the guesses are easy to find and change.
What was asked for: all nine tonebars, the upper manual only, the C3 chorus, and a band that works the swell pedal and the Leslie speed by itself. Not built: percussion, the lower manual, bass pedals, the other vibrato settings.


Three kinds, in falling order: technical write-ups read in full (Electric Druid, Scott Healy’s playing tips, Wikipedia); documents quoted in search results but not opened (the Hammond service text, Stefan Vorkoetter); and forum posts quoted in search results, where the link is to the thread the search named and the exact post was not checked (Keyboard Corner, Cantabile, Nord, Fractal). Anything resting only on the third kind is one player’s word.



Nothing is sampled. Each note is three oscillators, a few milliseconds of noise, and then one chain shared by all the notes.



Part
What it does
Where the numbers come from




Tonebars
Nine pitches for a key: 16′, 5⅓′, 8′, 4′, 2⅔′, 2′, 1⅗′, 1⅓′, 1′, at 0.5, 1.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 times the note
Electric Druid


Tonebar steps
0 is silent; each step from 8 down is 3 dB quieter
A clone’s description of the real instrument (Hammy 91); widely repeated, not from a Hammond document


Tempering
The fifths and the third are tempered wheels, not pure harmonics: 1.4988, 2.9976, 5.0409 and 5.9953 times the note. So a note is one oscillator for the octaves, one for the three fifths, one for the third
Electric Druid


Foldback
91 wheels. Key 1 (C2) takes its 8′ from wheel 13. A pitch above wheel 91 is taken an octave lower; the bottom octave’s 16′ an octave higher
Electric Druid (its table did not survive being read by machine; the rule here reproduces its wheel ranges)


Leakage
A closed tonebar still lets a trace through (−48 dB, octaves only)
That it exists: Electric Druid. The amount: a guess


Key click
A key’s nine contacts do not close together. Here: 22 ms of filtered noise as a note starts, with its own slider
The cause: Electric Druid. The sound of it: a guess


Touch
None. A note is the same level however it is played
Scott Healy: “the organ isn’t velocity-sensitive”


C3 chorus
A delay swept up and back 6.87 times a second (412 turns a minute), about 0.9 ms from end to end, mixed half and half with the straight sound
Rate and that the scanner runs up the line and back: Hammond service text. About 50 µs a stage over 18 stages: Stefan Vorkoetter (an M-100, not a B-3). The half-and-half mix: a guess; no source gives the real ratio


Swell pedal
Never silent: 24 dB down at its quietest. Keeps the bass up as it closes. Sits before the tube stage, so opening it also adds growl
That it never closes, lifts bass and treble as it comes down, and drives the amp harder as it opens: Nord forum, quoting a Hammond manual. The 24 dB and the 7 dB of bass: guesses; no source gives figures


Tube drive
The amp-chain drive already in the band, set low
A guess


Rotary speaker
Split at 800 Hz into a horn and a drum. Horn 48 turns a minute slow, 400 fast; drum 85% of that. Two microphones on opposite sides
Crossover and speeds: Wikipedia; 48 / 400 and 40 / 342 measured on a 147: Fractal forum


Speed changes
The horn gets most of the way in about 1.5 s, the drum in about 5 s
“Less than two seconds” and “4 to 10 seconds, depending on belt tension”: one forum post, found by search. No measured figure exists that I could find, so treat it as anecdote



Measured in tests/band/pat/organ.cdp.js: with every tonebar out, all nine pitches of A4 come out within 0.2 dB of each other; the 1⅗′ sits at 2218 Hz, not the pure 2200; C7’s 1′ sounds at 4186 Hz (two octaves folded back); two steps of a tonebar are 6.0 dB; the pedal closed is 24 dB down; the speaker moves the level 0.8 times a second slow and 6.67 fast, and summed to mono the swing all but cancels.



None of these is sourced. The searches named famous registrations (Jimmy Smith, Charles Earland, Groove Holmes, Erroll Garner, “full organ”) but gave no digits, so the menu describes each sound and attributes it to nobody. The default is 88 8000 000.



BandComp.organist decides, bar by bar, where the pedal sits and when the speaker changes speed. It uses no random numbers. Each rule, and what it rests on:
Swell pedal



Rule
Why




It follows how hard the band is playing: about half open when the band plays down, nearly open at full, a little more in a chorus
The organ has no touch, so the pedal is its only dynamics (Healy: “vary the dynamics using the expression pedal”)


The last bar of each four-bar phrase opens through the bar into the next one; more so going into a chorus
“Start with the expression pedal at minimum, then increase the pedal slowly”; a crescendo into the build (Healy)


The first bar of a phrase settles back a little
“Back off the pedal as the speaker slows down” (Healy)


A stop bar is hit and then pulled back sharply
“Pull the expression pedal back suddenly for a sforzando effect” (Healy)


The last chord swells and is let go
A guess



Leslie



Rule
Why




Slow is home
Rock and blues players “lean on that chorale mostly” (a forum post: Keyboard Corner or Cantabile)


Fast through the last bar of a phrase that leads into a chorus or back to the top, or that the band is playing hard; slow again as the next phrase starts
“As your single note starts to build, pop your Leslie or rotary switch to fast, and depress the pedal” (Healy). A forum player describes speeding up at the end of a phrase (Cantabile)


On a chord held two bars or more, a flick to fast for the second half of the phrase’s last bar and straight back
“Flip the Leslie to fast, then immediately flip it back to slow” under pads (Healy)


In swing the speaker stays slow, until the last two bars of the last chorus
Jazz players mostly leave the speaker alone and rely on the chorus (a forum post, Keyboard Corner or Cantabile: they “stop the horn entirely for the vast majority of work”). Slow, not stopped, is my choice


Fast on the final chord
A guess; a common ending



Thresholds that are mine: “playing hard” is an intensity of 0.66 or more; the flick lasts a beat and a half; the pedal’s range is 0.48 to 0.90 of its travel across the band’s intensity.
Nothing was found for gospel. The searches turned up no description of gospel pedal or Leslie habits, so the straight-eighth rules above are rock and blues habits applied to everything that is not swing.



Mixer → Organ: tonebars, swell and Leslie, shown while the organ is the comping instrument or the second one: nine tonebars, a registration menu, Leslie (Automatic / Slow / Fast / Stopped), Swell pedal (Automatic / By hand), key click. The chorus, the pedal’s range, the drive and the speaker’s own numbers are in Mixer → Tone (EQ), in the organ’s amp. Settings are kept in the browser (localStorage.btOrgan, and btAmp for the amp).




Percussion, the lower manual, pedals, V1 to V3 and C1, C2.
Tapering (each wheel’s own level across the keyboard), which a commenter on Electric Druid calls the main reason for the instrument’s scream.
Leakage between neighbouring wheels at other pitches; contact bounce note by note.
The cabinet: no reflections, no horn tone, one tube stage for both rotors.
Tonebar moves, chorus on and off, and registration changes are not played by the band: only the pedal and the speed.
The comping is the piano’s voicings. An organist’s held chords with a moving finger under a held top note (Healy, Ex. 2) are not written.





When do you reach for fast: into every chorus, or only the last one? On held chords? At endings?
In jazz, do you leave the speaker slow, stopped, or off altogether with the chorus doing the work?
Where does your foot sit when comping: about half, or lower? How far do you open into a chorus?
Your comping registration, and whether you change it between verse and chorus.
Chorus C3 always on, or only for some styles?

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
The twelve-bar blues is three four-bar phrases on three chords. Almost everything players have done to it since is one of a small number of moves: go to a chord sooner, approach a chord with its own dominant, split a dominant into a two-five, or replace a dominant with the one a tritone away. This lesson adds those moves one at a time. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays two choruses after a one-bar count-in. Section 8 has a tune written in notation, where the note that is sounding lights up. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
1. The three-chord blues
Four bars of I, two of IV and two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Every chord is a dominant seventh, including the home chord. That is the sound of the blues: a tonic that carries a flat seventh and does not need to resolve.



Listen for the two places the form turns. Bar 5 is the first move away from home. Bar 9 is the highest point of tension, and the last four bars walk it back down.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 2. The quick change and the turnaround
text:
2. The quick change and the turnaround
Two small changes, both very common. In bar 2 the band goes to IV for one bar and comes straight back (the quick change), which breaks up four bars of the same chord. In bar 12 the band plays V instead of resting on I, so the end of the chorus pulls into the top of the next one (a turnaround).



Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
text:
3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
Swing and bebop players turned the last line round. Instead of V then IV, they play ii7 then V7: the bass now moves by fifths (G, C, F in the key of F) all the way home. To set up the ii chord, bar 8 becomes VI7, the dominant of ii. The turnaround in bars 11 and 12 is the same idea at twice the speed: I, VI7, ii7, V7, two beats each.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 4. Getting to IV, and getting back
text:
4. Getting to IV, and getting back
Three more moves, each of them a way to make an arrival stronger.

Bar 4: a two-five into IV. The I7 chord in bar 4 is already the dominant of IV, so put its ii chord in front of it (v7 I7, two beats each).
Bar 6: the bass climbs a half step from IV to ♯iv°7, and that chord pulls back to I in bar 7. This one is as old as the blues on the piano.
Bar 8: split VI7 into its own two-five, iii7 VI7.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
5. Tritone substitution
A dominant seventh chord and the dominant seventh a tritone away share the same third and seventh (swapped). So either can stand in for the other, and the substitute’s root arrives by a half step from above instead of by a fifth. Here it is in four places: the end of bar 4 (♯IV7 falling to IV), the end of bar 8 (♭III7 falling to ii), bar 10 (♭II7 falling to I), and a turnaround built entirely of substitutes: I, ♭III7, ♭VI7, ♭II7.



Listen to the bass. Wherever a substitute is used, the line slides down by half step.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
6. The Bird blues
Charlie Parker’s “Blues for Alice” keeps only three landmarks of the form: I in bar 1, IV in bar 5 and the two-five in bars 9 and 10. Everything between is a chain of two-fives. Bars 2 to 4 descend by step to reach IV. Bars 6 to 9 descend by half step to reach ii. The home chord is a major seventh, not a dominant.



Compare it with the jazz blues of section 3. The shaded bars show how little is left.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
7. The minor blues
The same twelve bars with minor i and iv chords. The last line is usually ♭VI7 to V7: a dominant a half step above the dominant (the tritone substitute of V’s own dominant). The turnaround uses a half-diminished ii chord. “Mr. P.C.” and “Equinox” are both built this way.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the bass player’s chair, starting from one note per chord. You need to know how to fret a note and pluck it. Everything else is built here, one step at a time. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams read like a bass standing upright in front of you: the low E string is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear its notes. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff, and below the chord chart is the bass line the band is playing. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, the bar on the chart and the diagram of the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the bass and the band’s bass player stops so that you can take the part. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. A blues has three chords, so it has three roots, and they sit close together. Find the key note on the E string. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on the next string up. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on that same string. Your hand does not have to move.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.
Start with two notes in each bar, on beats 1 and 3.



Count the bars as you play: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. When that is steady, play the root on every beat. Press Superimposed to see all three roots on one fretboard.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
2. Root, fifth and octave
The fifth of a chord is one string up and two frets up from its root. The octave (the root again, higher) is two strings up and two frets up. Index finger on the root, ring or little finger on the other two: the three notes make a box that has the same shape on every chord. Move the box to each root you learned in step 1.



The band’s bass plays root on beat 1 and fifth on beat 3. Play that first, then try root, fifth, octave, fifth, one note to a beat.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
3. The 3rd and the 7th
The root and fifth say which chord it is but not what kind of chord. Two other notes do that job.

The 3rd says major or minor. In a dominant seventh chord (G7) it is a major 3rd: one string up and one fret back from the root.
The 7th in a blues chord is a flat 7th (written ♭7), a whole step below the octave: two strings up at the same fret as the root.

Together they are called the guide tones, because they are the notes that change the most tellingly from one chord to the next. Root, 3rd, 5th and ♭7th are the four chord tones. Click each chord’s name to hear them climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



The band’s bass plays exactly that: root, 3rd, 5th, ♭7th, one note on every beat, the same shape in every bar. The line is written out below the chord chart. It is not a walking line yet. It is the four chord tones in order, so that your hand learns each shape and your ear learns what each note sounds like against its chord.
Work up to it in three stages, each for a few choruses:

Root on beat 1, 3rd on beat 3. Two notes to a bar.
Root, 3rd, 5th, and rest on beat 4.
All four notes, as the band plays them.

Then switch to Superimposed and look at I and IV together. The 3rd of the I chord is one fret below the root of IV, and the ♭7th of I is one fret above the 3rd of IV. Those half steps are how the chords connect.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
4. Walking
In step 3 every bar went the same way: up the chord from the root. A walking line also has one note on every beat, but it chooses its notes so that each bar leads into the next. Three changes turn the step 3 line into a walking line: the notes after the root can come in any order, the octave joins them, and the last note of the bar points at the next root. A recipe that always works:

Beat 1: the root of the chord.
Beats 2 and 3: any two other chord tones (3rd, 5th, ♭7th, or the octave).
Beat 4: an approach note, one fret below or one fret above the root of the next bar’s chord.

When the next bar is the same chord, beat 4 can be any chord tone. The diagram shows the chord tones of all three chords at once. A split dot is a note two chords share.



Listen to the band’s bass player for a chorus, then tick Leave out the bass and walk it yourself. Slow the tempo down as far as you need. A plain line that lands on the root at every chord change is worth more than a busy one that does not.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord. Its 3rd is a minor 3rd, three frets above the root on the same string. Everything else about the shape stays the same.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Play the root on the beat each chord arrives and one other note after it: root and 3rd, or root and an approach note into the next root.

Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and walk through it with the recipe from step 4.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
This is how a guitarist plays chords in a band on a 12-bar blues without a single barre chord: two or three well-chosen notes, moved by a fret at a time. You need to know how to fret a note and how the strings are numbered (6 is the low E, 1 is the high E). For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams show the neck standing upright: string 6 is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear it. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its guitarist plays exactly the notes in the diagrams, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the guitar to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. Find the key note on string 6. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on string 5. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on string 5. Three chords, three notes, and the hand stays where it is.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.



Play one long note per bar with the band and count the form: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Knowing where the roots are is what lets you find every chord shape that follows.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
2. What the 3rd and 7th do
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. They do different jobs.

The root names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
The 5th adds weight and not much else.
The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Play only those two notes and a listener still hears the chord, especially with a bass player underneath. The diagrams show all four notes of each chord, with the guide tones filled in. Click a chord name to hear the four notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



From the root: the 3rd is one string up and one fret back, the 5th is one string up and two frets on, and the ♭7th is two strings up at the same fret as the root.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
3. Guide tones on strings 5 and 4
Now play just the 3rd and 7th, as a two-note chord on strings 5 and 4. Look at the Superimposed view to see what makes this worth learning: the three chords are the same two-finger shape, one fret apart. From the I chord, move both fingers down one fret for IV and up one fret for V.
That works because the 3rd of one chord is a half step from the 7th of the next. Going from I7 to IV7, the 3rd drops a fret and becomes the ♭7th, and the ♭7th drops a fret and becomes the 3rd. Switch the labels to chord tones and watch the two notes swap names.
Up a tritone. The 3rd and ♭7th of a dominant chord are six frets’ worth of pitch apart, an interval called a tritone, and a tritone turned upside down is still a tritone. So the same two-finger shape six frets higher gives the same two notes of the same chord, with the 3rd and ♭7th changing places. Press Up a tritone to move all three chords there. That gives every chord two homes on each pair of strings. In keys where the lower home would run off the end of the neck (F and G♭ here), the diagrams start in the upper one, so the three shapes always stay one fret apart.



The hollow dot is the root. Where one is shown it is in reach on string 6 and you can add it; where none is shown, leave it to the bass player.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
text:
4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
The same pairs one string set higher sit under roots on both low strings, so every chord can have its root added. These three-note chords are shell voicings: root, 3rd and 7th with the 5th left out. A chord with its root on string 6 has the 7th on string 4 and the 3rd on string 3. A chord with its root on string 5 has the 3rd on string 4 and the 7th on string 3. Mute string 5 with the side of your finger when the root is on string 6.
First the two notes alone:



Then with the root. This is the rhythm guitar sound of the swing era. Up a tritone here moves each chord to its other shell: the root changes string and the 3rd and 7th change places above it.



The band’s guitarist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm, then try four even strokes to the bar (set the feel and tempo to taste).

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is one fret lower than a dominant chord’s. In a shell with the root on string 6, that puts the 7th and the minor 3rd at the same fret, under one finger.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Press Superimposed to see how little the hand moves through ii7, V7 and I7.

The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Here are all four notes of each chord in the right hand, root at the bottom. The 5th is dashed because it is the first note to leave out. Click a chord name to hear the notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
3. Guide tones over a root
Now play only the 3rd and 7th in the right hand, with the root in the left. Look down the lanes: the right hand’s two notes hardly move. Going from I7 to IV7, each note drops a half step, and they swap jobs: the 3rd becomes the ♭7th and the ♭7th becomes the 3rd. For V7 both notes sit a half step above the I chord’s.
To keep the hand still, the two notes are not always in the same order. Sometimes the 3rd is on the bottom and sometimes the 7th. Switch the labels to chord tones to see which.



The band’s pianist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm once the changes are comfortable.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
4. Shells in the left hand
Put root, 3rd and 7th in the left hand alone and the right hand is free for a melody. A three-note chord with the 5th left out is a shell voicing. To keep the hand in one place the notes are rearranged from chord to chord, so the root is not always on the bottom.



Play a chorus of shells with the left hand only. Then add one note of your own in the right hand per bar. Any chord tone will do.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
5. Rootless voicings
When there is a bass player, the root is taken care of, and the left hand can spend its fingers on colour instead. A rootless voicing is the two guide tones plus two notes from higher up the chord: the 9th (a whole step above the root) and the 13th (the same note as the 6th). There are two forms, one with the 3rd on the bottom and one with the 7th on the bottom, and they alternate so the hand barely moves. This is the standard left-hand sound of jazz piano since the late 1950s.



The dashed square is the root, shown only so you can see where the voicing sits in relation to it. Leave it to the bass.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is a half step lower than a dominant chord’s. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide tones take turns to fall by a step: the 7th of each chord drops to become the 3rd of the next.



The same chorus with rootless voicings in the left hand:

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the drum chair, starting with nothing but the beat. You need to be able to hit the ride cymbal (or hi-hat), the snare and the bass drum, and to work the hi-hat pedal. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the beat written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a drum staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. Each step starts in its own feel and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
Reading a drum part
Each line or space of the staff is one part of the kit. Cymbals and anything struck on the rim are written with an ✕. What the hands play has stems up; what the feet play has stems down.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
1. The beat and the form
A drummer has two jobs on a blues: keep the time, and know where in the twelve bars the band is. Start with the plainest time there is. The ride cymbal (or the closed hi-hat) plays all four beats. The left foot closes the hi-hat on 2 and 4. Nothing else.



Count the bars out loud while you play: four bars, then four more, then the last four. The chords change at bar 5, bar 7 and bar 9. Listen for the bass moving and learn to hear those moments coming.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
2. The ride pattern
Swing time on the ride cymbal is the four beats plus a skip note just before beats 3 and 1: ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a. It is written as two eighth notes, but the first is long and the second short, as if the beat were divided in three and you played the first and last parts. Keep the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.



Listen with Drums alone to hear how late the skip note sits. Slow the tempo down and it gets later still.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
3. Swing time
Now the other two limbs. In swing the bass drum is played very quietly on all four beats, felt more than heard (feathering), and it is not written. The snare does not keep time: it answers the band with a note here and there, often on the last part of a beat. The band’s drummer improvises this, so the notation changes every chorus.



Start with the ride pattern and the hi-hat foot. Add one snare note per bar, on the “a” of beat 4, and leave it at that until it is comfortable.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
4. Showing the form
A fill tells the band where it is. On a blues the places to mark are the ends of the three four-bar phrases: bar 4, which leads to the IV chord; bar 8, which leads to the last line; and bar 12, which leads back to the top. The small ones need only a beat or two. The one in bar 12 can be bigger, and the crash on beat 1 of the next chorus is its landing.



Keep the time going right up to the fill and come out of it on beat 1. A fill that loses the beat is worse than no fill.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
5. The shuffle
The beat of Chicago blues. The cymbal plays the swung eighths all the way through, long, short, long, short, with the bass drum on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. This is the first beat on this page with a backbeat.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
6. The slow blues in 12/8
At a slow tempo every beat divides in three, and the cymbal plays all three parts. Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. It is written here in 4/4 with triplets; the same beat is often written in 12/8.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
7. Straight eighths
Not every blues swings. In a boogaloo or a rock blues the eighth notes are even. The cymbal plays eight to the bar, the bass drum is on 1 and 3, and the left hand plays a cross-stick on 2 and 4.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
This is the 12-bar blues for instruments that play one note at a time: violin, saxophones, and anything else with a single line. It starts with one note per chord and ends with a line that spells out a jazz blues. You need to be able to read notes in your instrument’s range. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom transposes the page. Violinists leave it on concert pitch. Alto and tenor players choose their saxophone, and every chart and line of notation is then written in their key, while the band plays in the concert key shown beside it. A B♭ tenor and an E♭ alto reading this page at the same time see different notes and sound the same ones.
How to use the page. Every step is a twelve-bar line. Under each note is the name of its place in the chord at that moment: R for the root, then 3, 5, ♭7. Press ▶ Play beside the notation to hear the line alone, or ▶ Play with the band to hear it over the rhythm section, where the piano plays it. Tick Leave out the melody to play it yourself. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation either way.
Sections 1 to 6 build the skills. Section 7 puts them to work on a tune, Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet. If you would rather start with the tune, go there first and come back.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after. A blues has three chords and three roots. Play each one as a long note and count the bars: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I.



A bass player would play these notes. Playing them yourself is the quickest way to hear where the form turns.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
2. Chord tones, and the 3rd and 7th
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord. Here are the four notes of each chord, played up from the root.



The 3rd and the 7th are the guide tones. They are the two notes that tell a listener which chord this is, and they are the notes a good melody leans on.

Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line. The explanation follows the key and instrument chosen in the strip at the bottom.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
3. Guide-tone lines
Play only a guide tone of each chord, and at each change move to the nearest guide tone of the new chord. The line barely moves: when I7 goes to IV7 the 3rd falls a half step and becomes the ♭7th of the new chord. One note per bar, and the whole harmony of the blues is in it.
Starting on the 3rd:



Starting on the 7th. Two players can take one line each.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
4. Guide tones in rhythm
The same notes become a background figure when they are given a rhythm. This one is the Charleston: a note on beat 1 and another on the “and” of 2. A horn section plays exactly this kind of thing behind a soloist.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
5. A riff
A riff is a short figure repeated through the form and adjusted to fit the chords. This one is the 3rd, 5th, 6th and 5th of the home chord. Over the IV chord only its first note changes: it drops a half step, which makes it the ♭7th of IV. Over the V chord the whole figure moves up to that chord.



Look at the names under the notes in bars 5 and 6. The fingers play almost the same thing, and every note has a new job.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord, with a minor 3rd. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide-tone line steps down: the 7th of each chord falls to the 3rd of the next.

section: 7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is over guide tones and a root.



The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a half step to become the ♭7th of IV, the same move your right hand makes. Once the guide tones are secure, play the riff in the right hand and rootless voicings in the left:

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford, who wrote this tune, was a bass player. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12 to turn it round. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, so the bass has room to be heard.



Play roots through the form first, two to a bar, and listen to how the riff sits against them. Then walk it. In bars 4 and 8 the melody holds one long note: that is the place for your line to lead clearly into the next chord. In bar 12, aim for the root of the V chord and then back to the top.

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is with the shells from step 4 underneath.



Comp under the tune with a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3, and leave the riff room. Then look at the guide tones alone. The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a fret to become the ♭7th of IV, which is exactly what your guide-tone shape does at the same moment.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
section: 7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford wrote this blues in the early 1950s. It is a riff blues: one two-bar idea, played three times over the twelve bars. Learn the first two bars and you know nearly all of it.




How it is built

Four notes. The whole melody uses the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. Look at the names under bars 1 and 2: R, 3, R, 4, 3, R.
Three lines. Bars 1 to 4, 5 to 8 and 9 to 12 are the same riff. Each ends on a long note, which is where the rhythm section answers.
Notes that arrive early. Several notes are tied across the barline. They are played an eighth note before the beat and held into the next bar. Clap the rhythm before you play it. These early notes are what make the riff swing.



The one note that changes
In bars 5 and 6 the riff’s second note is a half step lower than it was in bars 1 and 2. It is the only accidental in the tune. Over the home chord that note was the 3rd. The IV chord has that pitch a half step lower, as its ♭7th, so the melody moves with the chord. In bar 7 the home chord returns and so does the original note. This is the sound of a blues going to IV, and the melody tells you the chord has changed without any help from the band.
Hear that move by itself. This is the guide-tone line from section 3 on the tune’s changes. Play it, then play the tune again and listen for the same half step inside the riff.





The last line
Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five (ii7 then V7) instead of V then IV. The melody does not change at all, but look at the names under it: the same pitches are now the 9th and ♭7th of the ii chord. A riff this simple fits because every one of its notes belongs to the key.
The roots of the tune, to learn where the chords fall:





Practising it

Sing the riff with the band before you play it.
Play bars 1 and 2 alone until the tied notes sit right. Use ▶ Play beside the notation to check yourself.
Play the whole tune with Leave out the melody ticked.
Change the concert key. A riff you can play in three keys is a riff you know.

When the tune is secure, go on to the improvising lesson, which uses this melody as its starting point.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
section: 8. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues, at a medium swing. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and each time it ends on a long note, in bars 4, 8 and 12. Those are the same three places step 4 marked with fills. The tune leaves the space; the drummer fills it and sets up the next phrase.



Play time through the riff and stay out of its way: no snare on top of the melody’s accents. Read the melody while you play. A drummer who knows the tune plays the form without counting.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet is a good first tune because its changes are the three-chord blues with just two of the moves above.

Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five, ii7 then V7, as in the jazz blues of section 3.
Bar 12 is V7, the turnaround of section 2.

Everything else is plain. There is no quick change in bar 2 (four full bars of I), bars 5 and 6 are IV, bars 7 and 8 stay on I with no VI7, and bar 11 is one bar of I. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the three-chord blues of section 1.



The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and the note that is sounding lights up as it plays. Listen to bars 5 and 6: one note of the riff is a half step lower there than in bars 1 and 2, because the 3rd of the I chord has become the ♭7th of the IV chord. The changes are in the melody. In bars 9 and 10 the riff does not change at all, even though the chords under it are new: every note of it belongs to both the ii chord and the V chord.
To build this chorus yourself in the next section, choose Stay on I, Stay on I, Stay on IV, Stay on I, Two-five and V in the last bar. Open in the Backing Track puts the tune on that page in a new tab, where the bass line, comping and drums can each be chosen. The instrument lessons each end with this tune, and the improvising lesson is built on it.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
This lesson is about making up your own melody over a twelve-bar blues, using Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet as the model. It is for any instrument. You should already be able to play the tune (it is taught in Blues for Violin and Saxophone, section 7) and know what the chords are (Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues).
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom sets up the page for you.
Where this page says “concert”, it means the note as the piano hears it.
How to use the page. Every line of notation has a ▶ Play button, and the note that is sounding lights up. The chord charts have ▶ Play with the band; the piano plays the written line unless you tick Leave out the melody. Under each note is its place in the chord (R = root) or its number in the scale.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
1. Start from the melody
The best first solo on any tune is the tune. It already fits the chords, it already has a rhythm, and the listener already knows it.



Three things about this melody are worth stealing.

It is a riff. One two-bar idea, played three times. A solo built from one idea that is repeated and changed a little sounds like it means something. A solo of new ideas in every bar does not.
It uses four notes: the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. You do not need many.
It leaves space. Each line ends on a long note. Half of each phrase is silence or holding.

Exercise. Play the tune. Then play it again and change one thing: leave a note out, repeat a note, or play the rhythm of the riff on a single pitch. Keep the long notes where they are. Do that for several choruses before you go on.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
2. Hitting the change
The most important moment in a blues is bar 5, where the home chord gives way to IV. In this tune the melody marks it with one note. In bars 1 to 4 the riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord (concert A when the tune is in F). In bars 5 and 6 that note drops a half step (concert A♭), and it is now the ♭7th of the IV chord. In bar 7 it goes back up.
A soloist who plays the higher note in bar 5 sounds lost: it is a half step away from a note the chord needs. A soloist who plays the lower one sounds like they know the tune. That is what players mean by hitting the change (or making the change).
Here is that move alone: one note per bar, the 3rd or 7th of each chord, taking the nearest one at every change.



Exercise. With Leave out the melody ticked, improvise using only the rhythm of the riff and the notes of this line: the upper note in bars 1 to 4, the lower one in bars 5 and 6, the upper again in bar 7. It is very little to play with. Hit the change every time, exactly on bar 5, before you add anything else.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
3. The minor blues scale
Six notes, and it can be played over the whole twelve bars without changing anything. That is why it is the first scale most improvisers learn.



Counted from the key note it is R, ♭3, 4, ♯4, 5, ♭7. Two of those are blue notes:

The ♭3 is the same pitch as the note that hit the change in section 2 (concert A♭ in F). Over the IV chord it is a chord tone. Over the home chord it rubs against the chord’s major 3rd, and that rub is the sound of the blues.
The ♯4 is a passing note between 4 and 5. Slide through it; do not sit on it.

What this scale does not have is the major 3rd of the home chord. Played for a whole chorus it sounds dark and tough, and it never quite says which chord you are on.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
4. The major blues scale
The brighter one. Counted from the key note: R, 2, ♭3, 3, 5, 6.



It has both thirds: the ♭3 and the major 3rd, side by side. That is the same pair of notes the melody uses to hit the change. Sliding from the ♭3 up to the 3 is one of the most recognisable sounds in the music. This scale fits the home chord perfectly, because its 3, 5 and 6 belong to it.
It fits the IV chord less well. Its major 3rd is the note that section 2 told you to leave in bar 5.
Putting the two together. Use each scale where it is strongest:

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
section: 6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
text:
6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
The blues scales treat the whole chorus as one sound. The other way to improvise is to give each chord its own scale. A dominant seventh chord takes the Mixolydian scale: a major scale with the 7th lowered. Its 1, 3, 5 and ♭7 are the chord, and the notes between join them up. (Where that lowered 7th comes from is explained in the “flat 7” panel of the instrument lessons.)
For the home chord:



For the IV chord:



Compare them note by note. They share every pitch but one. The home chord’s scale has its major 3rd; the IV chord’s scale has that note a half step lower, as its ♭7. It is the same half step as in section 2, the one the melody plays. Hitting the change and changing scale are the same act.
For the V chord:

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The two-five: Dorian
Bars 9 and 10 are ii7 then V7. A minor seventh chord takes the Dorian scale: a major scale with the 3rd and the 7th lowered.



Now look back at the V chord’s Mixolydian scale above. It is the same seven notes, started from a different place. The ii chord and the V chord of a two-five share one scale, so bars 9 and 10 need only one set of notes, and the melody shows it: the riff passes over both chords unchanged.
That scale is also the plain major scale of the key. So the whole chorus comes down to three sets of notes, each one note different from the last:

Bars 9, 10 and 12 (ii7 and V7): the major scale of the key.
Bars 1 to 4, 7, 8 and 11 (I7): lower its 7th. That is the home chord’s Mixolydian.
Bars 5 and 6 (IV7): lower the 3rd as well. That is the IV chord’s Mixolydian.

To hear the notes that tell these scales apart, this line plays the ♭7, 6, 5 and 3 of every chord, one bar each:

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. Your chorus
Nothing is written here. The band plays the changes and the chorus is yours. Tick Loop in the strip at the bottom to keep it going.



A plan for practice, one item per session:

The melody, varied a little more each chorus (section 1).
Only the two notes of the change, in the riff’s rhythm (section 2).
Only the minor blues scale, in two-bar phrases with two bars of rest after each.
Major blues scale on the home chord, minor blues on IV, following the table.
Three major pentatonics: the root’s own, for whichever chord is sounding.
Chord scales: one chorus where every phrase ends on the 3rd or ♭7 of the chord of the moment.
Trade fours with the band: you play four bars, rest four, play four.

In every one of them, hit the change in bar 5.

text:
5. The pentatonic scales
Take the ♯4 out of the minor blues scale and five notes are left: the minor pentatonic.



Take the ♭3 out of the major blues scale and you have the major pentatonic.



Why bother with scales that have fewer notes?

Nothing in them clashes. Neither scale has a half step in it, so no two of its notes rub against each other, and any of them can be held. They are the safest notes there are.
They fall under the hand. On guitar and bass the minor pentatonic is the first position most players learn, two notes on every string. On a wind or string instrument it is five notes with no awkward corners.
The minor pentatonic covers the whole chorus, exactly as the minor blues scale does. Use it when you want to think about rhythm and phrasing and not about notes.
A major pentatonic built on a chord’s own root always fits that chord. It is the chord’s root, 3rd and 5th plus its 2nd and 6th: no 4th and no 7th, the two notes that cause trouble. So one more way through the form is three pentatonics: the home chord’s in bars 1 to 4, the IV chord’s in bars 5 and 6, and so on.
Two for the price of one. The major pentatonic of the key has the same five notes as the minor pentatonic that starts a minor 3rd below it. Compare the scale below with the major pentatonic above. If you know one shape, you know the other.




The blues scales are these two pentatonics with one extra note each: the ♯4 added to the minor, the ♭3 added to the major. Those added notes are the blue notes.
